question: Why does a 4-wide elementwise loop cost about 14% while a 2-wide one is free? Measured with no XLA anywhere, so the answer cannot be a compiler artefact.
design: An elementwise kernel over n floats (two reads, one write, a couple of multiplies, a max and a reciprocal), compiled by nvrtc through CuPy at the 128-thread block XLA itself uses. Total work is identical in every cell; only how many elements a thread owns, and which ones, changes. n = 1,368,900, exactly the element count of the reference lattice at B = 60.

schemes.blocked: thread t owns elements t*VEC .. t*VEC+VEC-1 (consecutive)
schemes.strided: thread t owns elements t, t+T, t+2T, ... (grid-stride, coalesced)

result.strided_4_vs_1: -45.3% time, 3571 GB/s, 107% of HBM3 peak (L2 helping)
result.jax_reference: +14.25% at width 4 and +0.09% at width 2, on Rd 23.55 L 3, H100
result.verdict: The blocked scheme at VEC=4 is the ONLY cell slower than VEC=1, and it costs +14.9% against the JAX kernel's +14.25% -- a match within 0.65 pp, reproduced with no compiler involved. The same width run coalesced is 45% FASTER, so width itself is not the problem: the problem is that XLA gives each thread CONSECUTIVE elements.

mechanism.note: Blocked, one load instruction across a 32-thread warp touches addresses 4*VEC bytes apart, so the warp's request spans VEC*128 bytes and needs VEC 128-byte transactions to deliver 128 bytes of useful data.
mechanism.crossover: Widening also cuts the block count and raises instruction-level parallelism, which is why VEC=2 blocked still wins by 27%. At VEC=4 the 4x transaction waste overtakes that gain and the sign flips. That is exactly the measured signature: width 2 free, width 4 expensive.

reconciles: The compiler-versus-hardware split was a false dichotomy. XLA makes the DECISION (which width, and consecutive rather than strided); the memory system sets the PRICE. That is why the penalty correlates with device properties and why experiment 3b's hand-written kernel was flat: 3b used one site per thread at every B, so no width decision ever varied. Forcing the width in raw CUDA brings the penalty back.

refuted_here.hypothesis: The ~2 MB footprint threshold is XLA's working set fitting in L2.
refuted_here.arithmetic: XLA's own allocation is 0.676 MB per replica (7.8x the spin array, from the 3a probe). At B=60 that is 16.4 MB for arm A and 40.6 MB for arm B. BOTH fit in the H100's 50 MB L2, yet arm A is null and arm B is +15%.
refuted_here.also: This probe touches 15.7 MB per pass -- comparable to arm A -- and the blocked VEC=4 penalty appears anyway. So arm A's null result is not explained by the coalescing picture either.
refuted_here.status: REFUTED. The footprint threshold remains open, but better posed.

still_open: Why arm A (16.4 MB working set) shows no penalty when this probe shows one at 15.7 MB. Something about the small-N lattices suppresses it.
Why B=512 is the global minimum and B=768 near the worst, both width 4.
Whether XLA picks blocked indexing on every target architecture.

method.note: sd below the timer's resolution in every cell
